result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about C9orf72-associated ALS/FTD, including that G4C2 repeat expansion is the most frequent genetic cause, that patients can have >1000 repeats while healthy individuals have <20, and that RAN translation produces five DPR species with poly-GA being most abundant.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C13-C18) are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. The claims provide appropriate context for the experimental work.

result: Prior work has shown that DPRs accumulate in both nuclear and cytoplasmic deposits, with poly-GA mainly cytoplasmic, R-DPRs accumulating in the nucleus (and nucleolus in cell models), though in patients R-DPRs are predominantly cytoplasmic with only rare para-nucleolar inclusions.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. C24 is additionally supported by experimental data in Figure 2B showing NLS-GA65-GFP aggregates excluded from nucleoli.

result: Synthetic GA65-GFP constructs form predominantly cytoplasmic inclusions with some nuclear foci, consistent with patient brain localization. Nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates are both amyloid-like but differ in structural properties: cytoplasmic aggregates are SDS-insoluble while nuclear aggregates are more soluble and show differential antibody accessibility.
evaluation: Claims C37-C53 are well-supported by multiple experimental approaches including microscopy (Figures 1B-D), amyloid staining (AmyT and OC antibody), p62 co-localization, and filter retardation assays (Figure 1E). The differential solubility is demonstrated with multiple targeting sequences and mutations, strengthening the conclusion.

result: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates (NLS-GA65-GFP) disrupt nucleolar structure by mislocalizing NPM1 from the granular component without affecting the fibrillar center marker RPA40, and impair nucleolar protein quality control as shown by failure of heat-stressed NLS-LS to repartition from nucleolus to nucleoplasm during recovery.
evaluation: Claims C55-C65 are supported by microscopy data showing NPM1 mislocalization (Figure 2A), normal RPA40 distribution (Figure 2B), and quantitative analysis of NLS-LS repartitioning defects (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The quality control assay provides functional evidence for nucleolar dysfunction.

result: Nuclear poly-GA (NLS-GA65-GFP) is significantly more toxic than cytoplasmic poly-GA (NES-GA65-GFP) in MTT viability assays. This differential toxicity is independent of targeting sequences or mRNA, as demonstrated by comparable expression levels, alternative targeting sequences (PY), alternative degenerated sequences, and rescue by mutations that disable nuclear targeting.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C66-C71 are strongly supported by viability data (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C) with appropriate controls including expression level verification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and multiple independent constructs. The experimental design effectively isolates compartment-specific effects.

result: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates (NES-GA65-GFP) partially impair nuclear protein transport as measured by S-mApple shuttling assay, causing mild defects in both import and export, though less severe than the β-sheet control protein NES-β17. Nuclear poly-GA aggregates have minimal effects on protein transport.
evaluation: Claims C74-C80 are supported by quantitative microscopy data (Figure 3) showing S-mApple distribution with and without leptomycin B treatment. The use of established controls (NES-β17, NLS-β17) and bidirectional transport measurements strengthen the conclusions.

result: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates potently inhibit TNFα-induced nuclear translocation of p65, similar to Huntingtin-exon1 control, while nuclear poly-GA has limited effect. The translocation defect is independent of upstream signaling as p65 phosphorylation and IκB degradation are normal.
evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by quantitative microscopy (Figure 4A-B) and immunoblot data (Figure 4C). The inclusion of Htt96Q as positive control and verification of normal upstream signaling strengthen the interpretation that transport machinery is specifically affected.

result: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates sequester importins α1 (KPNA2) and α3 (KPNA4), and to a lesser extent importin β1 (KPNB1), with enrichment at aggregate periphery, while nuclear poly-GA has no effect on importin distribution. Nuclear pore complexes remain properly localized.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 1B) with fluorescence profile analysis showing peripheral enrichment. The differential effects between cytoplasmic and nuclear aggregates are clearly demonstrated.

result: Synthetic poly-GA constructs (NES-GA65-GFP and NLS-GA65-GFP) have minimal effects on cellular mRNA distribution, in contrast to the β-sheet control protein NES-β17 which causes pronounced nuclear mRNA retention. This indicates poly-GA aggregates interfere with only a subset of nuclear transport factors.
evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by FISH data (Figure 5A-B) showing normal mRNA distribution with GA constructs versus strong retention with β17. The inference about selective transport factor interference (C99) is reasonable given the differential effects on protein versus mRNA transport.

result: G4C2-containing constructs (both NES and NLS targeted) form nuclear G4C2 RNA foci detected by FISH and cause nuclear mRNA accumulation in the majority of cells, independent of visible poly-GA protein aggregates. G4C2 RNA, not poly-GA protein, mediates mRNA retention.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by FISH data (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B) showing G4C2 RNA foci and mRNA accumulation only with G4C2 constructs, not synthetic GA constructs. The simultaneous visualization of RNA foci, mRNA, and protein aggregates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) provides strong evidence for RNA-mediated effects.

result: G4C2 constructs cause marked reduction in protein synthesis measured by OPP incorporation. Nuclear poly-GA (NLS-GA65-GFP) also reduces protein synthesis independently of G4C2 RNA, while cytoplasmic poly-GA has no effect. Cells expressing NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP (both RNA and nuclear poly-GA) show nearly complete translation inhibition, indicating additive effects.
evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by quantitative OPP incorporation data (Figure 5D-E) with cycloheximide control. The additive effect inference (C108) is well-supported by the observation that NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP shows greater inhibition than either component alone.

result: All G4C2 constructs (NES, NLS, untargeted) markedly decrease cellular viability independent of targeting sequence, indicating RNA-mediated toxicity. R-DPRs (PR73-GFP, GR73-GFP) expressed from synthetic constructs are not toxic despite detectable expression, while R-DPRs are undetectable from G4C2 constructs by immunoblot. The toxicity is attributed to G4C2 RNA rather than RAN-translated R-DPRs.
evaluation: Claims C109-C120 are supported by viability data (Figure 6A) showing toxicity of all G4C2 constructs and lack of R-DPR toxicity, immunoblot data (Figure 6B) showing undetectable R-DPR production from G4C2 constructs, and expression level controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). The logic connecting these observations to conclude RNA-mediated toxicity is sound.

result: The study demonstrates a multiple-hit model where G4C2 RNA is the predominant toxic agent causing mRNA export inhibition and protein synthesis defects, while DPRs exert additive but mechanistically independent effects. Cytoplasmic poly-GA impairs protein transport with little effect on viability, while nuclear poly-GA is more toxic, impairing nucleolar quality control and protein biosynthesis.
evaluation: Claims C3-C12, C121-C123 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple experimental results. The multiple-hit model is well-supported by the differential and additive effects observed across viability, transport, and protein synthesis assays. The conclusion that RNA effects predominate is justified by the greater toxicity of G4C2 constructs and lack of R-DPR production.

result: Both DPRs and G4C2 RNA interfere with different aspects of nucleocytoplasmic transport: G4C2 RNA inhibits mRNA export (independent of DPR aggregates), while cytoplasmic poly-GA partially inhibits protein transport. These effects are consistent with prior reports of transport factor sequestration and importin pathology in patients.
evaluation: Claims C125-C130 synthesize experimental findings with appropriate citations to prior work. The independence of mRNA export inhibition from DPR aggregates (C128) is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citations, though the contrast with Drosophila findings suggests model-specific differences.

result: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates are substantially toxic and form at sites distinct from nucleoli (similar to patient brain), causing nucleolar shape alterations through NPM1 mislocalization. The inhibitory effect on nucleolar quality control is comparable to R-DPRs, though R-DPRs may act by a similar mechanism in patients rather than direct nucleolar accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C135-C142 are supported by viability data (Figure 2D), microscopy showing nucleolar exclusion (Figure 2B), NPM1 mislocalization (Figure 2A), and quality control assays (Figure 2C). The speculation about R-DPR mechanisms in patients (C142) is appropriately cautious given the cited evidence that R-DPRs don't accumulate in patient nucleoli.

result: Expression of poly-GA from G4C2 constructs is substantially more toxic than from synthetic constructs at comparable protein levels. The major toxicity component is attributed to G4C2 RNA forming higher-order assemblies, as protein-only R-DPR constructs show no toxicity even at high expression levels, and prior studies could not distinguish RNA from DPR effects.
evaluation: Claims C143-C151 are supported by comparative viability data (Figure 6A), expression level controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), protein synthesis data (Figure 5D-E), and R-DPR detection (Figure 6B). The conclusion effectively addresses a key limitation of prior studies and is well-justified by the experimental design.

result: The authors conclude that G4C2 expansion interferes with multiple nuclear functions culminating in protein biogenesis inhibition that would be especially harmful to neurons. They acknowledge that DPR contributions cannot be excluded in patients with longer expansions and extended exposure, and that loss of C9ORF72 function might aggravate toxic effects.
evaluation: Claims C152-C158 represent speculative extrapolations to patient disease and neuronal vulnerability. While the experimental data support effects on nuclear functions and protein synthesis (C156), the implications for neurons (C157) and patients (C152-C153, C158) are not directly tested. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in the current study.

result: Prior work shows that G4C2 expansion can alter C9ORF72 protein expression, but knockout mouse models failed to fully recapitulate ALS/FTD phenotypes, suggesting loss of C9ORF72 protein is not the only contributor to pathology.
evaluation: Claims C25-C27 accurately summarize prior literature with extensive citations. The inference that loss of function is not the only contributor (C27) is reasonable given the incomplete phenotype recapitulation in knockout models.

result: Prior work has established multiple mechanisms of G4C2-mediated toxicity including: G4C2 RNA forming G-quadruplexes that sequester RNA-binding proteins and cause splicing defects; R-DPRs interacting with phase-separated compartments causing nucleolar stress; and cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates associating with proteasomes, interfering with proteasome activity, and inducing nuclear protein mislocalization.
evaluation: Claims C28-C36 provide comprehensive background on prior mechanistic studies with appropriate citations. These establish the context for the current work's focus on distinguishing RNA versus DPR contributions.

result: The manuscript cites prior work establishing that: the nucleolar granular component functions in protein quality control; artificial β-sheet proteins and disease proteins including poly-GA and R-DPRs interfere with nuclear transport; and aberrant mRNA distribution has been observed in G4C2-expressing cells and patient neurons.
evaluation: Claims C54, C59-C61, C72-C73, C87-C88, C94 appropriately cite prior literature including the authors' own work. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current experimental findings.

result: Synthetic R-DPR constructs (GR73-GFP and PR73-GFP) localize as expected based on prior reports: GR73-GFP predominantly in cytoplasm and nucleolus, PR73-GFP in nucleoplasm and nucleolus.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and consistent with cited prior work. This validates the R-DPR constructs used for toxicity comparisons.

result: The authors acknowledge that longer G4C2 expansions present in patients may have additional adverse effects not recapitulated with the 73-repeat constructs used in this study.
evaluation: Claims C124 and C145 represent appropriate acknowledgment of study limitations. While speculative, this caveat is important given that patient expansions can exceed 1000 repeats versus the 73 used experimentally.

result: Prior work has shown importin pathology in ALS/FTD C9orf72 patient tissue, and that other DPRs inhibit nucleocytoplasmic transport through mechanisms including poly-PR obstructing nuclear pores by binding FG domains and R-DPRs disrupting cargo loading onto karyopherins.
evaluation: Claims C131-C134 accurately cite prior literature on patient pathology and DPR mechanisms. These provide important context for the transport defects observed with poly-GA.

result: The endogenous C9ORF72 protein is thought to play a role in cellular quality control based on prior literature.
evaluation: Claim C159 appropriately cites prior work on C9ORF72 function. This provides context for the speculation about loss-of-function contributions to pathology.
